title: {{NAME}} and the Enchanted League
moral: Fair play is not just about rules, it is about the spirit behind them.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a shimmering aquamarine soccer jersey with small silver wings, white shorts, and aquamarine cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
Princess Beatrix had reformed the Royal Football League on one principle: radical inclusion.

New entrants this season: four fairy teams, two animal-player teams, a junior heroes side, and the standard human league members.

The rules were being revised by a committee.

{{NAME}} was on the committee.

The first problem on the agenda: the fairy teams could fly, which created issues around the offside rule, aerial possession, and the fundamental concept of staying on the ground.

pages.content:
Three days of committee work produced the Fairy Elevation Protocol: fairies could fly but must return to ground level before the ball crossed the goal line. Aerial ball-carrying was permitted within designated corridor zones.

The fairy representatives argued that this was complex. {{NAME}} argued that complexity served fairness.

"If your rules are simple but unfair, they're not good rules," he said.

Princess Beatrix was looking at him.

"He's right," she said. "Complex and fair is better than simple and excluding."

pages.content:
The season's matches were extraordinary.

Fairy teams at full flight in the designated corridors, human teams learning to defend against aerial transition, animal teams that were technically human-ruled but played with instincts no one could anticipate.

In {{NAME}}'s own match against the leading fairy team, he scored his goal by predicting exactly when they would drop to ground level: that split second of vulnerability at the zone edge.

He had read the Protocol three times and found the gap.

"You used the rules to beat us," said the fairy captain afterward, not unhappily.

"That's what rules are for," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The league finals were the most watched event in the kingdom's sporting history.

Princess Beatrix presented the trophy herself, to the winning fairy team, who had solved the ground-level requirement by training an aerial sprint that put them at ground level for exactly 0.4 seconds at the goal line.

{{NAME}} had watched them develop this technique all season and found it admirable.

"They found the solution inside the rules," he told Princess Beatrix.

"As did you," she said. "That's what makes a good league. Everyone finding their way within the same framework."

pages.content:
He walked home through the crowded post-match streets.

In the air above the city, small lights moved: fairy teams still playing informal games by lamplight.

On the park pitches, his own team was doing the same.

The rules had worked. The league had worked. Everyone had found their way within the same framework.

In bed, he could still hear the city, alive with the sound of a hundred different games being played under the same rules.

He fell asleep to that sound.
